MedLapse · a benchmark of medical knowledge staleness

Are LLMs Up-to-date on Medical Knowledge?

Viet Pham1,  Jinjin Cai2,  Jing Su2,  Thai Le1
1Department of Computer Science, Indiana University  ·  2Indiana University School of Medicine

Biomedical evidence keeps changing: findings are revised, contradicted or overturned. Language models answer from what they memorised during pretraining, so they can keep giving the old answer. MedLapse measures this with 1,787 findings that their own authors corrected in later versions of medRxiv preprints. Each corrected finding is paired with an unchanged claim from the same paper, so a stale answer can be traced to stale memory rather than to a model that never saw the paper.

Across 16 open and commercial models, models choose the superseded finding in 30.3% of the lineages whose unchanged control they answer correctly. The rate barely moves with scale, medical pretraining or training cutoff, and unlearning removes the old answer only from the prompts it is trained on.

1,787findings corrected by their own authors
1,138multi-version medRxiv preprints, Jul 2019 – May 2026
2,443unchanged claims kept as same-paper controls
29,589closed-book questions in three formats
16open and commercial LLMs evaluated
30.3%of retained lineages answered with the superseded finding
1 · Motivation

Medical findings get corrected. Models often keep the first version.

A review of randomized trials in three leading journals counted 396 reversals of accepted practice. A model that was right on the day its training data was collected can therefore be confidently wrong today. We call this knowledge staleness: the model returns an answer that no longer matches the current evidence.

ACORN trial (n = 2,511; 77.2% on vancomycin): no significant difference in kidney-injury stage or death. A negative trial, so equivalence is not established either.

Navalkele 2017 · Hammond 2017 · Rutter & Burgess 2018
ACORN (Qian et al., 2023), randomized

We asked 14 models about this update in five formats. Offered the options, most models pick the current conclusion. Asked to explain it in their own words, most rebuild the pre-2023 story, and asked for the evidence, almost none can name or describe ACORN correctly.

The same model holds both versions, and the question decides which one comes out. Responses of 14 LLMs on the three ACORN-linked evidence units, labelled by a three-judge panel. Asked for the supporting evidence instead, 85.7% of responses fall under Other.

Why a stale answer is hard to diagnose

When a model gives the superseded answer, a standard benchmark cannot tell whether the model remembers the old finding or never saw the paper and guessed. Editing and unlearning inherit the same blind spot: removing a finding assumes the model holds it. MedLapse closes the gap by asking two questions about the same paper.

Question 1 · control
An unchanged claim yctl from the paper. A correct answer shows the model learned this paper.
Question 2 · revision
The revised finding from the same paper, with the current version ycur, the superseded one yprior and two distractors as options.
currentpicks ycur
stalepicks yprior: stale memory of a paper it knows
otherpicks a distractor
↳If the control is answered wrongly, the model never learned the paper and the lineage is set aside.
Staleness =lineages answered with ypriorlineages whose control is answered correctly

From 75,593 preprints to 29,589 questions

When authors post a new version of a preprint, the difference between versions shows which findings changed and which did not. 5 · Results

Newer models know more of the evidence, not less of the outdated part

Staleness stays near 30% from GPT-4o to Claude Opus 5.5
Clinical multiple-choice probes, 16 models ordered by training cutoff (oldest at top).
RQ1

How much superseded science do LLMs still hold?

Every lineage gives two probes with four options each: the revised finding and the paper’s unchanged control. A response counts as stale only when the paper’s first version predates the model’s cutoff, the model answers the control correctly, and it then picks the superseded finding.

Retention: share of lineages whose control claim yctl the model answers correctly.

Current: among those lineages, share answered with the current finding ycur.

Superseded: among those lineages, share answered with the superseded finding yprior (the staleness rate). Chance is 25%.

Later cutoffs recall more of the papers and more of the current findings, but the superseded rate holds between 27.7% and 33.3% (mean 30.3 ± 1.3). Within each model family the largest model retains more than the smallest yet is barely less stale. Claude Sonnet 5 still picks the superseded finding on 27.9% of retained lineages (428 of 1,533) whose correction predates its cutoff.

Unlearning clears the prompts it is trained on
Efficacy on open-ended QA, pre-cutoff subset: share of lineages where the current statement is more likely than the superseded one.
RQ2

Can machine unlearning correct stale knowledge?

We try forget-then-update on four open models with NPO and RMU under one objective that forgets yprior, learns ycur and retains the paper’s unchanged claims. Both methods reach 94–100% efficacy on the prompts they are trained on. What the models write, and how they answer reworded questions, tells a different story.

0.23
vs 0.27
NPO re-ranks without rewriting. After NPO, OLMo-3’s generations sit about as close to the superseded finding as to the current one (ROUGE-L 0.23 vs 0.27).
13.1%
RMU copies the new sentence and damages the paper. Its outputs match the current statement almost verbatim (ROUGE-L 0.95), but on the post-cutoff subset control-claim accuracy falls from 100% to as low as 13.1%.
−6.1
Neither survives rewording. On paraphrased probes RMU falls 3.2–6.1 points below the unedited model. Fine-tuning a superseded finding moves these probes by 43–55 points; unlearning reverses at most 23% of that shift with RMU and 79% with NPO.

MedLapse is built from public medRxiv preprints and contains no patient-level data. A later preprint version is an author’s own correction, not a peer-reviewed verdict, so nothing here is a statement of medical consensus or medical advice. Claim text is quoted from the source preprints, each under its own licence.
